The Museum of Unfinished Things opened on a Tuesday because its founder had never managed to decide which Saturday would be best. There was no ribbon cutting. A length of red silk hung beside the entrance, along with a pair of scissors still sealed in their plastic packaging. The first visitor mistook this for an exhibit, which pleased the founder so much that she left it there. By closing time, someone had placed a small card underneath: *Ceremony, abandoned at the threshold.* Nobody knew who had written it. The handwriting was careful, but the final word sloped toward the floor.

The founder’s name was Mara. Before the museum, she had worked repairing clocks, a profession that gradually made her suspicious of completion. A repaired clock was never finished; it was merely prepared to begin failing again. Springs tired. Oil thickened. Teeth wore down. Customers returned carrying the same little boxes of interrupted time, apologizing as though they had personally disappointed the machinery. Mara would lift each clock to her ear and listen. Eventually, she began collecting what customers left behind: broken watches, unclaimed repairs, a wooden cuckoo whose owner had moved without giving an address. She liked keeping them company.

The collection grew through donations. A carpenter brought a chair with three legs, insisting that the missing fourth would have made it ordinary. A student delivered seventeen pages of a novel about a city where rain fell upward. Someone mailed a sweater with one sleeve, wrapped around a note that said, *He grew faster than I knitted.* There were shopping lists, architectural drawings, an engagement ring still attached to its receipt. Mara accepted almost everything. She refused only a jar labeled *Unfinished Thunderstorm*, because the lid looked unreliable and the museum’s insurance policy was already a matter of delicate negotiation.

At first, visitors laughed. They photographed a jigsaw puzzle missing every piece of the sky. They admired a landscape painting in which the mountains were magnificent but the foreground remained penciled instructions: *some sort of animal here*. Then, somewhere between the gallery of unsent letters and the cabinet of abandoned inventions, they grew quiet. Nearly everyone recognized something. A particular kind of delay. A hope postponed so politely that it had mistaken itself for a permanent arrangement. People stood before half-built boats and unrecorded songs with the expressions usually reserved for family photographs found unexpectedly in the backs of drawers.

A retired bus driver named Elias visited every Thursday. He always stopped at the same exhibit: two pages of music, the second ending halfway through a measure. The label identified it only as *Waltz, composer unknown*. After six weeks, Mara asked whether he could read music. “No,” he said. “My wife could.” She waited. “She used to play after dinner. Nothing impressive, according to her. I was impressed.” He pointed at the empty staves beneath the last notes. “I keep thinking this is where she would turn the page.” The following Thursday, Mara put a chair beside the glass case.

Not everyone approved. A newspaper critic called the museum “a monument to insufficient effort.” A council member asked whether celebrating incompletion might discourage children from doing their homework. Mara answered that they offered no position on homework, though the gift shop did sell notebooks with the final page torn out. This reply appeared in the newspaper without its accompanying smile. For several days, attendance doubled. People arrived prepared either to defend perseverance or denounce it. Most left distracted by a tiny pair of shoes, one finished, one still pinned together, donated by an apprentice cobbler who had later become a surgeon.

Mara had one object she never displayed. It lived in the bottom drawer of her office, beneath old invoices: a letter to her brother. They had quarreled years earlier over their father’s care, and then over money, and finally over which of them had started the quarrel. The letter began, *I have been trying to find the right way to say this.* Nothing followed. Sometimes she took it out and disliked its neatness. She had written those words on good paper with her father’s fountain pen, as though the materials might help her get further. They never had so far.

One winter afternoon, a child asked where the things went when people finished them. Mara explained that most donations stayed exactly as they were. “But what if somebody comes back?” the child persisted. “What if they know how now?” Mara looked toward the three-legged chair. She had spent considerable money protecting it from humidity. The child’s mother began apologizing, but Mara waved her quiet. That evening, she revised the donation agreement. Owners could reclaim their work whenever they wished. Within a month, the carpenter returned. He stood looking at his chair for a while, then asked to borrow a tape measure.

The museum changed slowly after that. A woman reclaimed a quilt and brought it back six months later, completed, to show Mara before giving it to her daughter. The student took home the upward-raining novel and returned only the binder. Elias asked whether a musician might play the unfinished waltz. Mara found a violinist who performed it on a Thursday afternoon. At the final note, her bow stopped. Nobody filled the silence. Elias nodded once, thanked her, and stayed in his chair until closing. The next week he came again, bringing biscuits for the staff and a better cushion for himself.

In spring, Mara took the letter from her drawer and crossed out its opening sentence. Underneath she wrote, *Are you still living above the bakery? I’ll be near there on Sunday. Could we have lunch?* She addressed the envelope before she could reconsider, then walked to the postbox without her coat. When she returned, a visitor was waiting outside the museum. He carried a cardboard box containing something wrapped in towels. Mara unlocked the door and helped him set it on the desk. “I’m not sure it belongs here,” he said. “Let’s have a look,” she answered, folding back the cloth.
